The Boids artificial life simulation was created by computer graphics pioneer Craig Reynolds in 1986.

He introduced the concept in his seminal 1987 paper, "Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model," published at the SIGGRAPH conference. The name "boid" is a shortened, stylized version of "bird-oid object."

Instead of using complex global scripting to control a massive group, Reynolds proved that complex, lifelike collective motion (like bird flocking or fish schooling) could emerge from individual agents following three incredibly simple local steering behaviors:

  • Separation: Steer to avoid crowding local flockmates (avoiding collisions).
  • Alignment: Steer toward the average heading of local flockmates (matching velocity).
  • Cohesion: Steer to move toward the average position of local flockmates (staying with the group).

This discovery was a massive breakthrough for both computer animation and complexity science, demonstrating how complex emergent behavior arises from simple rules. Reynolds actually won an Academy Scientific and Engineering Award in 1998 for his work, which paved the way for massive crowd simulations in films like The Lion King (the wildebeest stampede) and The Lord of the Rings.
